overview.text: The Confederate States of America (CSA), also called the Confederacy, was a breakaway government formed by Southern states that claimed to leave the United States during the Civil War. Seven states organized it at Montgomery, Alabama, before Abraham Lincoln took office in March 1861; after fighting began at Fort Sumter, four more slave states seceded, bringing its membership to eleven. Jefferson Davis served as its president. The Confederacy’s constitution resembled the U.S. Constitution but stressed state sovereignty, set a six-year presidential term, and protected slavery. Secession grew from conflict over slavery and fear that it would be restricted. The Union rejected secession’s legality, defeated the Confederacy in 1865, and preserved the United States as one nation.

key_facts.text: The Confederacy included eleven states: Texas, Arkansas, Louisiana, Tennessee, Mississippi, Alabama, Georgia, Florida, South Carolina, North Carolina, and Virginia.

Delegates from the first seven seceding states formed the government at Montgomery, Alabama, and selected Jefferson Davis as president; four more slave states seceded after fighting began at Fort Sumter.
Its Constitution, adopted March 11, 1861, resembled the U.S. Constitution but emphasized state sovereignty, allowed slavery in its territories, and set a six-year presidential term.
Slavery was central to secession: leaders feared the federal government would eventually end the institution on which their region’s economy depended.
The Union won the Civil War in 1865; the U.S. government did not accept secession as legally valid.
